papers.title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
papers.abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

papers.title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
papers.abstract: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

papers.title: Reconstructing hidden attractors with reservoir computing
papers.abstract: Hidden attractors are difficult to locate as their basins of attraction do not intersect with any small neighborhood of an equilibrium point. We examine the possibility of reconstructing the hidden chaotic attractor from time series via reservoir computing, where the reservoir is built by a network of driven Kuramoto oscillators. We compare all-to-all coupling, nearest-neighbour ring coupling, and a ring with one modified oscillator equation which ensures that any attractor will be hidden. The numerical results suggest that ring coupling supports accurate reconstruction over a wider range of coupling and forcing strengths than all-to-all coupling. Searches near reservoir equilibria nevertheless show why agreement in short-term prediction and long-term statistics does not establish preservation of hiddenness. Numerics for the modified ring show that it has the highest performance which coincides with our intuition that reconstructing the global dynamics would yield a more faithful attractor reconstruction. We also show that this construction precludes global forgetting of initial conditions for constant inputs, although local conditional contraction along a nonconstant signal remains possible. The distinction between reconstructing attractor dynamics and preserving basin structure provides a basis for evaluating and designing reservoir models of hidden attractors.

papers.title: Geometric encoding of turbulence for end-to-end quantum simulation
papers.abstract: Simulating multiscale turbulence in engineering remains challenging. Any quantum advantage for such simulations requires efficient initial-state preparation. Yet exact loading of an arbitrary classical snapshot requires exponential quantum resources. We introduce "turbuloscope", a physics-informed geometric method that generates statistically representative turbulent initial states in a gate-based register from a parameterized Pauli-spinor multiscale distribution. Scale invariance renders conditional rotations approximately affine in Gray-code space, enabling linear-depth, ancilla-free preparation. The generalized Madelung transform and Hopf fibration map the encoded Pauli spinor to fluid observables and vortex tubes. The qubit count scales logarithmically with the Reynolds number, yielding an exponential reduction in preparation overhead relative to full-grid classical spectral synthesis. We classically emulate a 30-qubit preparation circuit and generate a turbulent field over one billion grid points at a scale-inferred Reynolds number of 35,000, exhibiting Kolmogorov's five-thirds energy spectrum, tangled vortex tubes, and intermittency. This method provides scalable initial states for quantum simulation of turbulence and multiscale systems.

papers.title: Do Neural PDE Solvers Learn the Right Dynamics?
papers.abstract: Neural PDE solvers can achieve low prediction errors, but do they reproduce the dynamics of the systems they model? Prediction scores alone offer an incomplete answer: they measure agreement with reference solutions but provide limited insight into how errors accumulate, nearby states diverge, or extreme events arise. We propose an evaluation framework that directly examines these behaviors in deterministic and stochastic neural solvers. By evolving ensembles of nearby initial states and comparing them with direct numerical simulation, we assess three complementary aspects of learned dynamics: error formation, ensemble geometry, and extreme events. Experiments on two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow reveal limitations that conventional scores can obscure. Smaller trajectory errors can reflect weaker error amplification despite less accurate local updates. Models can match an ensemble's overall spread and effective dimension while failing to capture the spatial directions where nearby states diverge. Similarly, matching overall event frequencies can conceal failures to predict persistent extreme events. These findings show that improved prediction accuracy does not necessarily imply greater dynamical fidelity. Our framework makes this distinction measurable, providing concrete criteria for evaluating whether advances in neural PDE solvers better capture the underlying dynamics.
